title.en: The Broken String: Lament for the Rain-Magician

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Broken String'

summary.en: \xa-ttin's lament for his dead friend \kui-ten, the magician and rain-maker who died of a shot received while going about by night in the form of a lion. Now the string is broken, the sky's former ringing sound is heard no more, and the place does not feel as it used to feel.
summary.zh: 夏丁悼亡友庫伊滕——雨巫與術士，夜行獅形中槍而亡。弦既斷，昔日天際鳴響不復聞，此地亦不復如舊之感。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lament dictated by Dia!kwain (heard from his father) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: People were those who Broke for me the string. Therefore, The place became like this to me, On account of it, Because the string was that which broke for me. Therefore, The place does not feel to me, As the place used to feel to me, On account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 (public domain).

passages.text: For, The place feels as if it stood open before me, Because the string has broken for me. Therefore, The place does not feel pleasant to me, On account of it. Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: the above is a lament, sung by \xa-ttin after the death of his friend, the magician and rain-maker, \kui-ten; who died from the effects of a shot he had received when going about, by night, in the form of a lion.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 237 note; not verbatim.

title.en: !nuinumma-!kwiten: The White-Mouth Who Kills Crying Children

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of !nuinumma-!kwiten'

summary.en: A beast of prey of the early race, his name 'White-Mouth' — he who gobbled eggs whole. Hearing a child cry he follows the sound, creeps to the hut, springs in, catches the child and swallows it. Grandfathers sang his song to frighten noisy children into silence.
summary.zh: 早期之民猛獸，名「白嘴」——吞蛋不嚼者。聞童啼即循聲潛至，躍入茅屋，擒童吞之。祖父輩唱其歌以懾鬧童。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San ogre-song dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text:
u
umma-\kwiten formerly said (sang) — 'Hn-n, hn; I kill children who cry; Hn-n, hn. I kill children who cry.' A beast of prey (he, 
u
umma-\kwiten) is. My grandfather used to say (that) 
u
umma-\kwiten formerly said — 'Hn-n, hn; I kill children who cry.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 239 (public domain).

passages.text: The narrator gave the following explanation of \nu\numma-\kwiten's name: 'A man who eats great (pieces of) meat, he cuts them off, he puts them into his mouth. I think that eggs are white; therefore, I think that his name seems to be White-Mouth... Reference is here made to a man of the early race, who swallowed ostrich eggs whole, and is the chief figure in a legend related by \han≠kass'o (V.—56.).'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 239 note (public domain).

passages.text: And (when) he hears a little child crying there, he follows the sound to it, while the little child is crying there, he, following the sound, goes to it, approaches it stealthily, approaching stealthily, reaches the hut, in which the little child is crying. He springs, springs into the hut. He catches hold of the little child, he springs, taking it away. He goes to swallow it down. He departs.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 241 (public domain).

title.en: The Bustard's Head in the Fire: Why the Knorhaan Cries
title.zh: 鴇首入火：冠鴇啼聲之由

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Bustard'

summary.en: When the bustard (knorhaan, Brandkop) was still a man, his head was thrust into the fire by his brother-in-law, to punish him for having surreptitiously married a sister. Since then he is only a bustard: flushed red of head, crying 'wara \khau' when he flies and 'a wa, a wa' when he stands.
summary.zh: 冠鴇本為人；因偷娶其姊妹，遭妹夫將其頭按入火中。自兹為鴇：頭赤如火，飛時啼「瓦拉哈烏」，立時鳴「阿瓦」。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song-legend dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: My younger brother-in-law, Put my head in the fire. My younger brother-in-law, My younger brother-in-law, Put my head in the fire. When we startle it up, it flies away; it (cries): 'Wara \khau, wara \khau, wara \khau...!' When it stands on the ground, it says: 'A wa, a wa, a wa, a wa!' when it stands on the ground.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: when the 'Knorhaan Brandkop' was still a man, his head was thrust into the fire by his brother-in-law, in order to punish him for having surreptitiously married a sister. Since then he is only a bustard.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 233 note; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cat's Song: Derided by the Lynx

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Cat's Song'

summary.en: The cat sings its own mockery — 'I am the one whom the Lynx derides, I am the one who did not run fast' — as it goes along doubling in flight; the cat talks with its tongue and sings with the upper part of its mouth.
summary.zh: 貓自唱其辱：「獰貓嘲我，我不善走」——且行且唱，逃時迴折而走；貓以舌語，以口上顎而歌。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Ha ha ha, Ha ha, I am the one whom the Lynx derides, I am the one who did not run fast; For, the Lynx is the one who runs fast. It did foolish things; For, the Lynx is one who understands, The Cat does not understand. The Cat (nevertheless) is cunning. It had to be cunning. For, the Lynx is one who is cunning. Reference is here made to the Cat's way of doubling when pursued.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 221 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 222 (public domain). / Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 222 with note (public domain).

title.en: The Song of the Springbok Mothers

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Song of the Springbok Mothers'

summary.en: The springbok mothers sang, soothing their children — 'A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me' — a lullaby from the fable of the Anteater, the young Springbok, the Lynx, and the Partridge.
summary.zh: 羚母哄幼而歌：「阿——哄，跳羚之童！為我安眠。」此歌出自食蟻獸、幼羚、獰貓與鷓鴣之寓言。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lullaby dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Springbok mothers sang (soothing their children) — 'A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me. A-a hn, O Springbok Child! Sleep for me.' Condensed paraphrase of the editor's note: this song occurs in the fable of the Anteater, the young Springbok, the Lynx, and the Partridge (IV.—42.), in which the anteater carries away the young springbok and the mother sings to it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 235 (public domain). / Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 235 note; not verbatim.

title.en: The Old Woman's Song: The Hyena That Carried Her Off
title.zh: 老嫗之歌：負其而去之土狼

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1871 and 1873 (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Old Woman's Song'

summary.en: Left in an old hut by her starving people, an old woman too weak to walk is carried off by the hyena; she springs aside, beats it, and the hyena kills itself casting itself on the pointed rock. From the hyena's flesh she grows strong enough to follow and reach her people while they are still starving.
summary.zh: 族人饑而遷，老嫗留於舊屋；土狼負之而去。她躍避擊之；土狼自投尖岩而死。食其肉，婦力復，追及飢困之族人。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San song-story dictated by !A!kunta and ||kabbo to Bleek and Lloyd; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The old Woman sings; goes singing along; sings as she goes; the old Woman sings as she goes along about the Hyena — 'The old she Hyena, Was carrying off the old Woman from the old hut; The old Woman in this manner, She sprang aside, She arose, She beat the Hyena. The Hyena, herself, The Hyena killed the Hyena.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 229 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's 1875 summary (§80): an old woman who was too weak to walk was left behind by her people, when they, to escape starvation, travelled to another part of the country. She was afterwards picked up by a hyena and carried off to the mountain on its back. But she contrived to kill it, and finding an old pot, she cooked and ate some of its flesh. From this, she became so strong that she followed her people, and arrived in good condition among them, while they were still starving.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §80; not verbatim.

title.en: The Falling Star and the Hammerkop's Tidings

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Death'

summary.en: When our heart falls, a star falls with it; the stars know the time at which we die. The hammerkop flies crying 'yha! yha!' to tell of a death; its story must be sunk in the Orange River, where the stars stand in the water like fires — for the water is a pool in which we see all things, even the dead whom the Rain has taken, become flowers.
summary.zh: 吾心墜時，星隨之墜；星知人死之時。鎚頭鸛飛啼「呀！呀！」以報喪；其訊須沉入奧蘭治河——星立水中如火。水乃映照萬物之池，包括雨所攜之少女——化為水中之花。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The star does in this manner, at the time when our heart falls down, that is the time when the star also falls down; while the star feels that our heart falls over. Therefore, the star falls down on account of it. For the stars know the time at which we die. The star tells the other people who do not know that we have died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 389 (public domain).

passages.text: The people say: 'Did ye not hear the hammerkop, when the star fell? It came to tell us that our person is dead.' The people speak, they say that the hammerkop is not a thing which deceives, for it would not come to our home, if it did not know... it intends to come and tell us about it, namely, that our person has died.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 391 (public domain).

passages.text: Mother and the others used, — if they heard a hammerkop, when it flew, going over us, — to say: 'Do thou go and plunge in, for I know that which thou earnest to tell me'; while mother and the others said that the story, which it came to tell, should go into the Orange River's water, where the stars stand in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 391-392 (public domain).

passages.text: For, mother and the others used to tell us about it, that girls are those whom the Rain carries off; and the girls remain at that water, to which the Rain had taken them... The Rain lightens, killing them; they become stars, while their appearance has been changed... a girl, when the Rain has carried her off, becomes like a flower which grows in the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 393-395 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Rain's Thunderbolts and the Flower-Girls of the Water

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Death', pp. 393-397

summary.en: Girls whom the Rain has killed become flowers standing in the water; we must not pick them, for when we go toward them they sink. And when the Rain lightens, we must quickly look at the place of the flash: our eye also shines like its thunderbolts, and the Rain fears our eye and passes over.
summary.zh: 為雨所殺之少女成為立於水中之花；不可摘之，近之則沉。雷起時，須速視其閃處：吾目亦如雷石而閃，雨畏吾目，遂掠頂而過。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: Mother and the others used to tell us about it, that we ought not to go to the flowers which we see standing in the water, even if we see their beauty. For, they are girls whom the Rain has taken away, they resemble flowers; for they are the water's wives, and we look at them, leaving them alone.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 395-396 (public domain).

passages.text: The flower — when it saw that we went towards it — would disappear in the water. We should think: 'The flowers which were standing here, where are they?'... It would disappear in the water, when it saw that we went towards it; we should not perceive it, for it would go into the water.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 396-397 (public domain).

passages.text: For they are afraid that the Rain also intends, lightening, to kill them. For the Rain is a thing which does in this manner when it rains here, it smells our scent, it lightens out of the place where it rains. It lightens, killing us at this place; therefore, mother and the others told us about it, that when the Rain falls upon us and we walk passing through the Rain, if we see that the Rain lightens in the sky we must quickly look towards the place where the Rain lightens.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 397 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The Rain, which intended to kill us by stealth... if its thunderbolts have come near us, (if) we look towards the place where it has lightened... we look, making its thunderbolts turn back from us; for our eye also shines like its thunderbolts. Therefore, it also appears to fear our eye... Therefore, it passes over us on account of it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 397 (public domain).

title.en: Our Wind, Our Gall, and the Moon That Carries the Dead
title.zh: 吾風、吾膽與負死者之月

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Relations of Wind, Moon, and Cloud to Human Beings after Death'

summary.en: At death our own wind blows and makes clouds; the wind erases our footprints so the dead may not seem to live. Our gall sits green in the sky; our hair makes clouds. And the hollow moon carries the newly dead in its bowl — dying people are laid in it until it fills, then they descend and live again like the Moon, save that the Hare broke the bargain.
summary.zh: 死時吾風自吹而成雲；風抹吾跡，免似生者。吾膽懸碧於天；吾髮化雲。半月如匙，承載新死者——月盈而滿，死者下地復生如月；惟野兔毀約，死亡遂定。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San death-lore dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The wind does thus when we die, our own wind blows; for we, who are human beings, we possess wind; we make clouds, when we die. Therefore, the wind does thus when we die, the wind makes dust, because it intends to blow, taking away our footprints... our footprints, which the wind intends to blow away, would otherwise still lie plainly visible.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 397-398 (public domain).

passages.text: And, our gall, when we die, sits in the sky; it sits green in the sky, when we are dead. Therefore, mother was wont to do thus when the moon lying down came, (when) the moon stood hollow... The hair of our head will resemble clouds, when we die, when we in this manner make clouds.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 398-400 (public domain).

passages.text: Mother spoke, she said: 'The moon is carrying people who are dead. For, ye are those who see that it lies in this manner; and it lies hollow, because it is killing itself (by) carrying people who are dead. This is why it lies hollow... A person is the one who has died, he whom the moon carries. Therefore, ye may expect to hear what has happened, when the moon is like this.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 399-400 (public domain).

passages.text: We, who do not know, we are those who think in this manner, that (they) are clouds. We, who know, when we see that they are like this, we know that (they) are a person's clouds; that they are the hair of his head... while we feel that we seeing recognize the clouds, how the clouds do in this manner form themselves.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 400-401 (public domain).

title.en: The Man Who Cut Open His Wife for Greed

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore and other Texts (1875), §112

summary.en: A woman's darker mirror of faith: a man, believing his wife had been greedy, cut her open — and found, with great distress, that she was with child. He tried in vain to repair the harm by pinning her together with a stick, thinking she would live.
summary.zh: 男子疑妻貪食，剖其腹——惶然發現其有孕。以木針縫合，冀其能活，終不可救。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San tale dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1874; contains domestic violence and pregnancy death; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Bleek's summary (§112): a man cut his wife open, because he believed that she had been greedy, and then discovering, with great distress, that she was with child, tried in vain to repair the harm he had done, by pinning her together with a stick, thinking that she would live.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the same locus: whilst the principal death-story of §112 touchingly illustrates an old man's conception of a woman's faithful nature, and her husband's trustfulness and charity, another tale shows a woman's idea of a man's stupidity and distrust of his wife.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of A Brief Account of Bushman Folk-lore (Bleek 1875), §112; not verbatim.

title.en: Cutting the Little Finger, Piercing Ears and Nose

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) custom; recorded 1871 and 1884 (Bleek & Lloyd archive)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'Cutting off the Top of the Little Finger, and Piercing Ears and Nose'

summary.en: A boy has the top joint of the little finger of his shooting hand cut off — it is thought to make children live to grow up, and is done with a reed before they have sucked at all; the girl's left hand is cut for her female arm. Men pierce both ears; a woman with a pierced nose is handsome.
summary.zh: 男童截其射箭手小指之上節——俗信可保兒長成，以蘆葦為之，在吮乳之前；女童截左手，其女性之臂。男子穿雙耳；穿鼻之婦乃美。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San customs recorded by Bleek and Lloyd, 1871/1884; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A little boy has this hand cut. A female child has this hand cut, because she is a little girl, therefore, she has the hand of her female arm cut; because this is her female hand. Thus, the boy has this arm cut, with which they intend him to shoot; therefore, he turns this (the right) hand, when he grasps the arrow, he turns this (the left) hand, when he grasps the bow.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 329 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the 1884 account and note: the joint is cut off with a reed. It is thought to make children live to grow up. It is done before they suck at all. \xaben-an further explained that her father cut off the upper joint of his daughter Kaueten-an's little finger; and her husband cut off (the upper joint of) \kabbe-ttu's finger.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 330; not verbatim.
